desc_base1: You answer the phone, reboot routers and hear "it doesn't work" 40 times a day.
desc_base2: You create accounts, reset passwords and install stubborn printers.
desc_base3: The tricky tickets land on your desk: crashing PCs, moody VPNs, lost emails.
desc_base4: You patch cables, configure switches and start to understand the company network. Soon you'll have to pick your specialty.
desc_admin5: You manage Windows and Linux servers and make sure everything stays green.
desc_admin6: VLANs, routing, DHCP, DNS: you are the network.
desc_admin7: You design multi-site networks and set up high availability.
desc_admin8: You design tomorrow's infrastructure: datacenter, cloud and redundancy.
desc_admin9: You lead a team of admins and manage the hardware budget.
desc_admin10: Chief Information Officer: all of the company's IT is your responsibility.
trackdesc_Admin: Servers, VLANs, firewalls and backups: you keep the infrastructure running, all the way up to CIO.
desc_cyber5: You watch security alerts and sort real incidents from false alarms.
desc_cyber6: You investigate incidents: logs, malware, compromised accounts.
desc_cyber7: You get paid to hack the company (legally) and find the flaws before the bad guys do.
desc_cyber8: After an attack, you analyze disks and memory to find out what the hacker did.
desc_cyber9: You design the security of the whole information system: segmentation, MFA, zero trust.
desc_cyber10: Chief Information Security Officer: when a cyberattack hits, you're the one they call.
trackdesc_Cyber: Alert analysis, penetration tests and crisis management: you protect the company from hackers, all the way up to CISO.
desc_dev5: You fix bugs and write your first features, guided by the seniors.
desc_dev6: You build complete features, from the database to the interface.
desc_dev7: Front end, back end, APIs, databases: you do it all.
desc_dev8: You lead the team, review code and choose the technologies.
desc_dev9: You design application architecture: microservices, performance, security.
desc_dev10: Chief Technology Officer: you set the technical strategy for the whole company.
trackdesc_Dev: From your first "Hello world" to running the tech department: you build applications, all the way up to CTO.
career_desc: From the helpdesk to the boardroom: troubleshoot, configure, secure and code. After level 4, choose your path: Network Administrator, Cybersecurity or Software Development.

Did you know? In the middle of a crisis, there's no time to think: you need a plan ready in advance.
card91_text: Management asks: "If we get hacked tomorrow, what do we do?"
card92_opt0_res0:
{0.SimFirstName}'s team wins the CTF! §500 bonus.

Did you know? CTFs (like on Root-Me) are perfect for practicing legally.
card92_opt0_res1:
No win, but a lot learned.

Did you know? Even losing a CTF helps you improve.
card92_opt1_res0:
Someone has to watch the alerts!

Did you know? The SOC keeps running even during events.
card92_text: The company is holding a CTF (an ethical hacking competition) between teams.
card93_opt0_res0:
The "delivery person" was a real one… but the rule is reminded to everyone.

Did you know? "Tailgating" means getting in by following someone with a badge.
card93_opt0: Check the cameras and the logbook
card93_opt1_res0:
The same "delivery person" comes back and steals a laptop.

Did you know? Physical security is part of cybersecurity.
card93_text: A colleague lent their badge to a "delivery person" who wanted to get in.
card94_opt0_res0:
The VPN starts automatically: his data is protected.

Did you know? A hacker can create a fake Wi-Fi with the same name ("evil twin") to spy on connections.
card94_opt0: Make the VPN mandatory outside the office
card94_opt1_res0:
His credentials are intercepted on a fake Wi-Fi…

Did you know? On public Wi-Fi, always use a VPN.
card94_text: An employee often works from a café's free Wi-Fi, without a VPN.
card95_opt0_res0:
Hidden cryptocurrency mining software! {0.SimFirstName} removes it and finds the flaw.

Did you know? "Cryptojacking" uses other people's machines to mine cryptocurrency.
card95_opt0_res1:
{0.SimFirstName} removes the software, but can't find how it got in.

Did you know? If you don't find the cause, the attack will come back.
card95_opt1_res0:
Mining resumes right after the reboot.

Did you know? Malware often restarts by itself (persistence).
card95_text: A server runs at 100% CPU at night, even though nobody is using it.
card96_opt0_res0:
With a real attack as an example, management understands and approves the budget.

Did you know? To convince, talk about risks to the business (money, reputation), not technology.
card96_opt0_res1:
Management sticks to its decision. {0.SimFirstName} has them sign a risk acceptance.

Did you know? When management accepts a risk, it's recorded in writing.
card96_opt0: Explain the risk with a concrete example
card96_opt1_res0:
The flaw is exploited three months later…

Did you know? A pentest report is useless if nothing gets fixed.
card96_text: The pentest found a critical flaw, but management wants to postpone the fix "until next year".
card97_opt0_res0:
The disk was encrypted with BitLocker: the thief can't read anything.

Did you know? Disk encryption protects data if the computer is lost or stolen.
card97_opt1_res0:
It wasn't encrypted, and it held client contracts…

Did you know? A personal data breach must be reported to the data protection authority.
card97_text: A director's laptop was stolen on the train.
card98_opt0_res0:
Employees love it! They report twice as many suspicious emails.

Did you know? Well-trained users are the first line of defense.
card98_opt0_res1:
Nice, but a bit long.

Did you know? Short, regular training works better than one long session a year.
card98_opt0: Run an interactive quiz with real examples
card98_opt1_res0:
Half the room falls asleep.

Did you know? Nobody remembers a boring training session.
card98_text: {0.SimFirstName} has to lead a security awareness training session.
card99_opt0_res0:
Only the necessary traffic gets through now. The network is much safer.

Did you know? A well-configured firewall blocks everything by default and only allows what's needed.
card99_opt0_res1:
A business application stops working: a rule was missing.

Did you know? List the required traffic flows before tightening the rules.
card99_opt1_res0:
The firewall is useless as long as this rule exists.

Did you know? Overly broad rules are one of the most common mistakes.
card99_text: Reviewing the firewall, {0.SimFirstName} finds a rule "Source: any, Destination: any, Allow".
card100_opt0_res0:
If a camera gets hacked, the hacker can no longer reach the servers.

Did you know? Segmentation limits how far an attack can spread. Connected devices are often poorly secured.
card100_opt0: Split into zones with a firewall between them
card100_opt1_res0:
A hacked camera becomes an entry point to the whole network.

Did you know? A "flat" network lets a hacker move around everywhere.
card100_text: At the company, PCs, servers and cameras are all on the same network.
card101_opt0_res0:
The vendor never called: it was a scam attempt.

Did you know? Always call back using a number you found yourself, not the one the caller gave you.
card101_opt0: Call the vendor back on the official number
card101_opt1_res0:
The "technician" disables the firewall and disappears…

Did you know? Urgency is a classic pressure tactic used by scammers.
card101_text: Someone calls {0.SimFirstName}: "I'm the technician from your firewall vendor, give me admin access for an urgent update."
card102_opt0_res0:
Everything is logged and timestamped: the answer comes in 5 minutes.

Did you know? Centralized logs (in a SIEM) keep a record even if a hacker wipes the server's own logs.
card102_opt1_res0:
The audit flags a serious lack of traceability.

Did you know? Without logs, it's impossible to know what happened after an attack.
card102_text: An auditor asks who logged into the HR server last month.
card103_opt0_res0:
Access only to their server, with two-factor authentication and logging.

Did you know? Many attacks come in through a less secure supplier (a "bounce" attack).
card103_opt1_res0:
The supplier gets hacked… and the hacker walks into your network with their account.

Did you know? Least privilege applies to suppliers too!
card103_opt1: Give them an admin account, it's simpler
card103_text: A supplier is about to get network access to manage some software.
card104_opt0_res0:
The director understands and goes through an approved IT policy.

Did you know? Messages marked as "personal" are protected, even on company equipment.
card104_opt1_res0:
An employee files a complaint. The company is in the wrong.

Did you know? The CISO also advises on legality, not just on technology.
card104_text: The director wants to read employees' personal emails "for security".
card104_title: The Boss Wants to Watch Everything
card105_opt0_res0:
The alert was real: the vendor had been hacked. The network is spared.

Did you know? Checking a file's signature and hash makes sure it hasn't been tampered with.
card105_opt0_res1:
False alarm, the update was clean. A day's delay, no big deal.

Did you know? Always cross-check several sources before concluding.
card105_opt1_res0:
The malicious code spreads to every PC…

Did you know? Updates are rolled out to a small test group first.
card105_text: An update to a well-known program seems to contain malicious code, according to an alert online.
card106_opt0_res0:
A clear policy: which data can and can't go into an AI. Everyone gets it.

Did you know? What you send to an online service may be stored elsewhere: be careful with sensitive data.
card106_opt1_res0:
A confidential document ends up stored with an outside service…

Did you know? New technologies also create new risks.
card106_text: Employees are pasting confidential documents into an online AI to summarize them.
card107_opt0_res0:
The QR code led to a fake login page that stole passwords. Nobody fell for it.

Did you know? A QR code is just a hidden link: check the address before typing anything (quishing).
card107_opt1_res0:
{0.SimFirstName} types their password on the fake page… Everything has to be changed urgently.

Did you know? Never test a suspicious link with your real account.
